section.title: Wives and Husbands
section.sectionRationale: Peter completes the household teaching by turning to marriage. Wives and husbands, like citizens and servants before them, are shown how the gospel reshapes their relationships under pressure. The passage prizes an inner beauty precious to God, points wives toward winsome witness, and calls husbands to honor their wives as fellow heirs of grace.
section.thesis: In Christian marriage the gospel produces a wife whose gentle, godly conduct can win even an unbelieving husband and whose unfading inner beauty is precious to God, and a husband who lives considerately with his wife, honoring her as a fellow heir of the gift of life so that nothing hinders their prayers.
section.frameNote: Two movements: wives and the unfading beauty of a gentle spirit, verses 1 to 6; and husbands honoring their wives as fellow heirs, verse 7.

verses.text: Wives, in the same way, {{hypotasso|submit yourselves}} to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the {{anastrophe|behavior}} of their wives
when they see your pure and reverent demeanor.
Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes,
but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a {{praus|gentle and quiet spirit}}, which is precious in God’s sight.
For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands,
just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.

units.label: Husbands honoring their wives
units.note: fellow heirs of the gift of life

verses.text: Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate {{skeuos|vessel}}, and with honor as {{synkleronomoi|fellow heirs}} of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.

hypotasso.gloss: To submit, to place oneself under. Peter uses the same word for citizens, servants, and now wives, always as voluntary submission offered for the Lord's sake. Here it serves a missionary aim: a wife's respectful conduct may win an unbelieving husband. It is glad ordering within marriage, not the erasing of her dignity or worth.

anastrophe.gloss: Manner of life, conduct, behavior. A recurring word in the letter, it names the visible pattern of daily living that others observe. Peter says a wife's pure and reverent conduct can preach without a word, so that an unbelieving husband is won by what he sees more than by what he is told.

praus.gloss: Gentle and quiet, describing a spirit that is meek and settled, not weak but strong in restful trust. This inner disposition is the unfading beauty precious in God's sight. Far from timidity, it is the calm strength of a heart that hopes in God and does not give way to fear.

skeuos.gloss: A vessel or container. Peter calls the wife a delicate vessel, to be treated with care and consideration. The image is not of inferiority but of value and honor, like a precious vessel handled with tenderness. Husbands are to live knowingly and gently with their wives, honoring rather than harming.

synkleronomoi.gloss: Fellow heirs, co-inheritors. Husband and wife share equally in the gracious gift of life, the inheritance of salvation. This spiritual equality grounds the husband's call to honor his wife. Before God they are joint heirs, and to dishonor a fellow heir of grace is to hinder one's own prayers.

basic.context: Peter now speaks to married believers. To wives, especially those with unbelieving husbands, he says: let your godly, respectful life do the preaching, so your husband may be won without a word. Do not chase after outward beauty, braided hair, gold, fine clothes, but cultivate the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which God treasures. He points to Sarah and the holy women who hoped in God. Then, briefly but powerfully, he turns to husbands: live with your wife thoughtfully, treat her with honor as a precious vessel and a fellow heir of eternal life, or your prayers will be blocked.
basic.hermeneutics: This is part of the wider household teaching, so it must be read alongside the calls to citizens and servants, all shaped by living faithfully as exiles in a watching world. The submission is voluntary and Godward, and it is balanced at once by the husband's duty to honor his wife as an equal heir. We must distinguish the abiding principles, godly character, mutual honor, spiritual equality, from the cultural forms, such as first-century adornment. And note the sober warning: how a husband treats his wife affects his relationship with God.
basic.originalLanguages: Wives hypotasso, submit, so their anastrophe, their conduct, may win an unbelieving husband. Their true beauty is a praus kai hesychios spirit, gentle and quiet, precious to God. Husbands honor their wives as a delicate skeuos, vessel, and as synkleronomoi, fellow heirs, of the gift of life.
basic.typology: Sarah and the holy women of old model hope in God and quiet strength, and Peter says believing wives are Sarah's children, joining the family of faith that traces back to Abraham. The unfading inner beauty contrasts with all that perishes, pointing to the imperishable inheritance and the new creation where God's people shine.
basic.christ: The pattern of winning others by godly conduct rather than force echoes Christ, who did not retaliate but overcame by righteous suffering. The gracious gift of life that husband and wife share as fellow heirs is the salvation secured by Christ. His self-giving love is the deep model behind honoring a spouse as a precious fellow heir.
basic.god: God treasures what the world overlooks: a gentle and quiet spirit is precious in His sight. He is the one in whom the holy women hoped, the giver of the gracious gift of life shared by husband and wife, and the God who hears prayer, so that a husband's treatment of his wife touches his fellowship with God. He values inner character and honors both partners as heirs.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5 gives the fuller pattern of Christlike love in marriage. Genesis 18 and 21 recount Sarah, the mother of the faithful. First Samuel 16 says God looks on the heart, not outward appearance. And Galatians 3 says heirs together, male and female, are one in Christ.
basic.oneStory: God has always been forming a people marked by faith and inner beauty rather than outward show, from Sarah hoping in God to the church awaiting the gift of life. Marriage among believers puts that gospel on display, husband and wife as fellow heirs, honoring one another as they journey together toward the inheritance Christ secured.

context.literary:
The passage is one panel in a longer household teaching that Peter opens at 2:13 with a single governing verb, submit. Citizens (2:13-17), household servants (2:18-25) and now married partners (3:1-7) each receive the same opening, 'in the same way', and the whole sequence closes in 3:8 with a word to everyone. Read alone, the lines to wives can sound like a freestanding rule. Read in sequence, they are one more case of how an exile lives under pressure without losing his or her witness.

The proportions are telling. Wives receive six verses, husbands one. Yet the one verse is dense, a single sentence with two participles, two manners of living (with consideration, with honor), a purpose clause about prayer, and a double picture of the wife, as a vessel and as a fellow heir. Peter spends most of his words where the social risk was greatest, on the believing wife of an unbelieving man, who could be exposed to ridicule or worse for her faith.

Within the wives' section the movement is from conduct to adornment to example. Verses 1 and 2 state the aim, a husband won by watching. Verses 3 and 4 set two kinds of beauty against each other, braided hair, gold and clothing on one side, the hidden person of the heart on the other. Verses 5 and 6 supply a cloud of witnesses, the holy women of old, with Sarah as the named example.

Notice how 'behavior' and 'see' bracket the first two verses: they will be won by the conduct they observe. Nothing is said about arguing, preaching or ultimatums. The grammar of the sentence is built around a husband's eyes, not his ears. The second paragraph answers it in kind. As a wife's conduct is to be seen, so a husband's treatment of her has a consequence that only God sees, the hindering of his prayers, which is why the last line of the verse feels like a seal on everything that came before.
context.historical:
In the Roman world a household was the unit of society, and its head was expected to set its religion. Moralists of the period, Plutarch among them, taught that a wife should worship her husband's gods and keep her own religious devotions private. A woman who adopted a foreign faith, and above all one that Roman opinion already distrusted as a superstition, could be seen as undermining the order of the home. This is the pressure behind Peter's words. These wives lived in houses where their devotion to Christ was a visible affront, and Peter does not tell them to hide it but to let their character carry it.

The comment on adornment pictures the fashion of the day. Elaborate hairstyles, gold ornaments and costly fabric signaled status and wealth, and Paul gives a parallel instruction in 1 Timothy 2:9-10 for the same reason. Neither apostle bans taking care over appearance. They contrast a display that points to the self with a character that points to God, and they borrow the voice of Israel's wise men, who said in Proverbs 31:30 that charm is deceptive and beauty fleeting.

The law of the day left a wife with little standing, so verse 7 is more striking than it first sounds. A husband was legally the stronger party, and Peter bases his duty not on law or custom but on a shared inheritance and on God's attention. He assumes that the husband is a believer, and the unequal power he describes is exactly what the call to honor must restrain.

Sarah belongs to a world still older. She left her home, travelled with Abraham and was twice taken into other men's households, Genesis 12:10-20 and Genesis 20, so the hope that Peter commends in her was exercised in danger and uncertainty. Peter sets that ancient picture beside the first-century church to say that this kind of faith is not new and not modern; God's people have lived it for as long as there has been a promise.
context.canonical:
The first thing the passage does canonically is to take up the Old Testament's picture of true beauty. Proverbs 31:30 sets the fear of the LORD against passing charm, and 1 Samuel 16:7 records that God looks on the heart, not on outward appearance. Peter's 'hidden person of the heart' stands in that line, and so does Paul's matching word in 1 Timothy 2:9-10. The passage is a New Testament application of an old and consistent teaching, not a new rule.

Peter's holy women draw on the whole sweep of Genesis. Sarah is the one he names, from Genesis 18:12, where she speaks of her husband as her master while laughing at the promise. That might seem an odd choice of proof text, but Peter has the broader story in view, in which Isaiah 51:2 calls Israel to look to Abraham and to Sarah who gave them birth, and Hebrews 11:11 counts Sarah among the faithful. The apostle is calling these wives her daughters in faith.

Husbands and wives are also drawn into the wider New Testament teaching on marriage. Ephesians 5:21-33 opens with mutual submission and then sets out love like Christ's for the church as the husband's measure, and Colossians 3:18-19 gives a shorter form of the same pair. Paul's 1 Corinthians 7:12-16 speaks directly to the situation of a believer married to an unbeliever, hoping the believing partner may be a means of grace, which is Peter's own hope in verse 1.

The phrase 'fellow heirs' gathers one of the most important threads in the New Testament. Romans 8:17 calls believers co-heirs with Christ, and Galatians 3:28-29 says that in Him there is no male and female, all being Abraham's offspring and heirs by promise. Peter applies that truth where it is hardest to live, in the most intimate household relationship, and says that it has consequences for prayer, which Jesus Himself linked to reconciliation in Matthew 5:23-24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wrote to Christians who were being slandered as troublemakers and who had to decide how to answer. His purpose here is practical and pastoral. He wants wives married to unbelievers to know that their quiet faithfulness is not wasted and not weak; it is the means by which God may win a husband. He wants them free from the idea that they must either hide their faith or force it on an unwilling spouse.

He also wants them to know where their dignity lies. The world they lived in prized display, and a wife's worth was often measured in her husband's eyes by her appearance and her obedience. Peter tells them that God measures differently. The gentle and quiet spirit is not a description of a timid woman; it is called precious in God's sight, and that is a verdict with weight far beyond anything a household could give.

The single verse to husbands is the other half of the same concern. Peter will not let the instruction to wives be heard as a license. A man who has authority in the home, and who may be tempted to use it, is told to live with understanding, to honor and to remember that his wife shares his inheritance. He is told that his own prayers depend on it.

The first hearers were meant to leave with two convictions. One was that their ordinary married life was part of their witness to a watching world. The other was that no one in a Christian home, in whatever role, stands on a lower rung with God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nearly everything here is instruction, not narrative, so the question is not what was merely recorded but how far the commands travel. Peter's counsel to wives with unbelieving husbands answers a particular situation, and its principle, that a life of visible goodness can persuade where argument fails, applies wherever believers live among people who do not share their faith. The details of braided hair, gold and clothing belong to the first-century setting, but the contrast between display and character does not.

The language of submission has to be handled with care. Peter commends it as a voluntary act of a person who hopes in God, and the same verb is used of every Christian's posture toward rulers, masters and elders in 2:13, 2:18 and 5:5. It is not an account of a woman's nature, nor permission for a husband to demand obedience, nor an instruction to endure abuse. The very next verse limits what a husband may do with whatever authority he has.

Sarah is an example of faith, not a template for every detail of speech. The passage does not command a wife to use the word 'lord'; it points to her hope in God and her refusal to be ruled by fear.

What the church should carry forward without hesitation is the pairing: character that is gentle and strong, honor that is real and costly, and an understanding that husband and wife are one in the grace that matters most.

debates.question: How should the call for wives to submit be understood today?

views.label: An enduring pattern of ordered, mutual honor
views.case: Peter's submission is voluntary and Godward, set within a marriage where the husband must honor his wife as a full equal heir. The pattern of loving order remains, never as domination but as part of mutual, Christ-shaped honor.

views.label: Culturally framed but rooted in gospel witness
views.case: Others stress the missionary and cultural setting: the counsel aims at winning unbelieving husbands in a specific society, so its abiding core is godly conduct and honor rather than a rigid hierarchy. Even so, it never licenses a husband's dominance.

debates.bearing: Both readings insist that this passage dignifies wives, treats them as equal heirs, and condemns any harsh or dishonoring treatment. Whatever the structure, mutual honor and Christlike love are non-negotiable.

debates.question: What does it mean that a husband's prayers may be hindered, verse 7?

views.label: Broken fellowship disrupts prayer
views.case: A husband who dishonors his wife, a fellow heir of grace, damages his own communion with God, so his prayers are obstructed. God takes seriously how we treat those made in His image and joint heirs of life.

views.label: A sober warning tied to God's justice
views.case: Others hear a stronger note: God will not lend His ear to a man who mistreats his wife. The warning underscores that private conduct in marriage is never hidden from God and directly affects one's standing before Him.

debates.bearing: Both agree that how a husband treats his wife matters immensely to God, so much that it touches his prayer life. Honor in the home and fellowship with God are bound together.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb to notice is the one translated 'submit yourselves' in verse 1, a participle that hangs on the command of 2:13 rather than standing as a fresh imperative. Peter uses the same stem for citizens before the king, 2:13, for household servants, 2:18, and for the young before elders, 5:5. Its picture is one of arranging oneself in an order, and it is said of Jesus Himself, who in Luke 2:51 was subject to His parents. In the middle voice the action is the person's own, which fits the sense of a free, Godward choice. The same word comes back in verse 5 for the holy women.

The word the BSB renders 'behavior' is a favorite of this letter. Peter uses it at 1:15, 1:18, 2:12, 3:1, 3:2 and 3:16, always for the whole manner of a life seen from outside. He asks for it to be holy, to be honorable among the Gentiles, to be pure and reverent in a wife and good in Christ. The word is what others see; the word 'see' in verse 2 is the matching verb.

The two adjectives for the spirit in verse 4 deserve a slow reading. One is the word Jesus uses of Himself in Matthew 11:29, 'gentle and humble in heart', and the same word appears in Matthew 5:5 and in Paul's list of the Spirit's fruit in Galatians 5:23. The other, 'quiet', is used in 1 Timothy 2:2 for the settled life believers pray for. Neither word names weakness. They name a self under control and a heart at rest in God, 'precious in God's sight', a phrase that sets the value in His eyes against every other judge.

In verse 7 Peter writes that husbands should dwell with their wives 'according to knowledge', which the BSB renders 'with consideration'. The sense is of a husband who learns his wife and acts on what he knows, and who does not live by assumption or habit. The 'weaker vessel' in older translations is a description of physical vulnerability in a world that offered a woman little protection, not of intellect or faith. The same noun appears in Romans 9:21 and 2 Timothy 2:20-21 for household vessels of different kind, and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 for the jars that hold a treasure. 'Fellow heirs' is a single compound word, found also in Romans 8:17 and Hebrews 11:9, and it makes the point that what a wife receives from God is the same as what her husband receives.

The last clause, 'so that your prayers will not be hindered', uses a verb of cutting in or blocking, the same family of word Paul uses of being hindered from coming to Rome, Romans 15:22. Prayer is the road, and mistreatment of a wife is the barrier.

typology.fulfillment: Sarah is the matriarch of the people of promise, and Peter says believing wives are her daughters if they do right and refuse to give way to fear. The correspondence is of family and faith: the church inherits Abraham's household, Galatians 3:29. The escalation is that Sarah received a promised son after waiting, and believers receive the promised Son Himself, born of a woman, Galatians 4:4. The type falls short in that Sarah's faith had faltering moments, Genesis 18:15, while believers stand on the finished work of Christ.

typology.type: The imperishable beauty of the hidden person
typology.fulfillment: Peter sets an adornment that does not fade against hair, gold and clothing that do. The same contrast of perishable and unfading frames his opening praise of an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, 1:4, and of faith more precious than gold that perishes, 1:7. The pattern is fulfilled in the new creation, where the people of God are clothed with the glory of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-8. The comparison is a lesson in value, not an allegory of every ornament.

typology.type: The husband as the one who yields power for love
typology.fulfillment: A husband with authority is told to honor his wife as a fellow heir. That shape is fulfilled in Christ, who held all authority and used it to give Himself up for the church, Ephesians 5:25, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-8. The husband's love is a small echo of the large pattern. The type falls short because no husband can save his wife; Christ alone gives His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45.

typology.type: A household where prayer is shared
typology.fulfillment: The picture of husband and wife as heirs of the gracious gift of life points to the household of faith as a place of access to God, which Hebrews 10:19-22 describes as the new and living way opened through the flesh of Christ. In Him the family is not only a social unit but a small sanctuary where prayer is heard. The correspondence is partial, since the household is a sign of the church and not a replacement for it.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly through the example He gave. In the paragraph just before it, Peter has held up Jesus as the One who, when abused, did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 2:21-23. The wife with a hostile husband is invited into that same path. Her quiet conduct is not passivity but a share in the way Jesus overcame, a goodness that lets God vindicate. The word 'same' in 'in the same way' ties the marriage teaching back to the cross, so that the home becomes one more place where the pattern of the Suffering Servant is lived.

It leads to Him by the shape of authority He modeled. Peter tells a husband to honor, and Paul spells out what that means by pointing to Christ, who loved the church and gave Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25. The One who held all power used it to serve and to die. Any husband who reads 'head' as a right to be served has not read Christ, since in Mark 10:45 the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

It leads to Him by the inheritance. 'Fellow heirs' only makes sense because of Christ, who is the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, and whom believers join as co-heirs, Romans 8:17. A husband and wife stand equal in the one thing that matters, and their equality is a gift from the Firstborn who shares His inheritance with all who are in Him. The 'gracious gift of life' is that salvation, secured by His death and resurrection.

It leads to Him by the matter of prayer. Believers pray through Christ, Hebrews 4:14-16, and Jesus taught that reconciliation with a brother comes before an offering, Matthew 5:23-24. A husband whose prayers are hindered by his harshness is a man whose access is troubled by his failure to reflect the One through whom he prays.

A guard against forced reading is useful here. Sarah is not a hidden picture of the church, nor is a wife's submission to be read as a symbol of the church's submission to Christ in every detail. What the text supplies is Christ as the pattern of the quiet strength that overcomes without force and the One whose love is the measure of every husband's honor. That is enough, and it is a good deal.
study.god:
This short passage tells us a good deal about God. He is, first, a God who looks at what the world overlooks. A gentle and quiet spirit is precious in His sight, and the letter uses the language of preciousness elsewhere for the living cornerstone, 2:4-6, and the blood of Christ, 1:19. The things God values are not those that bring prestige. He sees a wife in a home where her faith is mocked, and He calls what she carries precious.

He is the God of hope. The holy women 'put their hope in God', and Peter treats this hope as the engine of their conduct. The God of Sarah and Abraham keeps promises over decades, and those who wait on Him are not put to shame. A believer who lives under pressure can rest in a Lord who knows the end of the story and who is able to turn a hostile husband's heart, as Peter hopes in verse 1.

He is the giver of the 'gracious gift of life'. The phrase puts grace first and life as the content. Salvation is not earned by either spouse, and neither can claim to deserve it more than the other. Because God gives it, no husband can boast, and no wife may be treated as less.

He is attentive to prayer. The warning in verse 7 assumes a God who hears, who cares who is praying and what is happening in the room before the prayer begins. The God who inclines His ears to the righteous, as Psalm 34:15 says, is moved by justice in the home. This is not a transaction in which good treatment buys a hearing; it is a picture of a Father whose children's relations with each other matter to Him.

He is the God who holds a tension together. He calls for submission and honor in the same breath, order and equality, quiet and strength. Peter does not resolve this by diminishing either side.

For worship, the passage invites us to find our worth where God finds it, and to bring our households into His presence, asking Him to make them places where His grace is practiced, not only believed.

crossReferences.note: Paul sets the same pair of instructions inside a call to mutual submission out of reverence for Christ. His longer account roots a husband's love in Christ giving Himself up for the church, which supplies the measure that Peter's single verse of honor assumes.

The scene behind Peter's picture of Sarah. She is old, laughing to herself at the promise, and then afraid when challenged. Peter does not pretend she was flawless; he chooses her because her story shows hope in God holding even through doubt and fear.

When Samuel looks at Eliab's height, the LORD says that man looks on outward appearance but He looks on the heart. This is the standard behind Peter's inner beauty, and it shows that his point is a very old one in Israel.

In Christ there is neither male nor female, and all who belong to Him are Abraham's offspring and heirs. This undergirds Peter's 'fellow heirs' and explains why the household instruction cannot be read as a ranking of worth.

Paul tells women to adorn themselves with modesty and good deeds rather than braided hair, gold, pearls or expensive clothes. The parallel shows that Peter's concern was not a single church's problem but a common apostolic teaching about where true adornment lies.

Paul speaks to believers married to unbelievers and hopes the believing partner may be a means of grace. He also lets the believer go if the unbeliever leaves. It shows the same pastoral situation as Peter's, with a realistic account of what is and is not in the believer's power.

Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. The wisdom tradition of Israel already measured a woman's worth by her reverence for God, which Peter takes up and applies to women under pressure.

Just before the household teaching Peter shows Christ as the One who, abused, entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge. The wife who responds to harshness with purity and respect is following that example, and the connecting words 'in the same way' make the link.

Believers are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. This is the larger inheritance that Peter's phrase 'fellow heirs' reaches for, and it makes the equality of husband and wife a reflection of their shared place in Christ.

Jesus tells the worshiper to leave his gift at the altar and be reconciled with his brother first. The pattern, that right relations on earth precede acceptable approach to God, stands behind the warning that a husband's treatment of his wife can hinder his prayers.

study.oneStory:
The passage answers a question that the opening chapters of Genesis leave hanging. Genesis 2 closes with a man and woman who are one flesh and unashamed, and Genesis 3 shows the fracture. The woman's desire and the man's rule are bent, Genesis 3:16, and from then on marriage carries a wound. Peter's words are not an attempt to restore Eden by rules. They show what a household looks like when redeemed people live together in a world still under the curse, with gentleness replacing contest and honor replacing mastery.

The story of Israel stands behind the example. Sarah lived under the promise and waited for what only God could give. Peter makes the line of faith run from her to a first-century wife in a hostile home, and says the family is one. What mattered then and matters now is hope in the God who keeps His word.

The passage also sits inside Peter's account of an exiled people, chosen and holy, living among those who do not understand them. Their homes are a front line of witness. A husband won without words is a picture of the gospel's way of spreading, not by force but by a life that makes others ask a question, as 3:15 will say.

The arrival of Christ changes what a family is. In Him a household is no longer only a social order but a place where two people receive the same gift of life, so the inheritance is shared rather than divided. This is a partial return of what Genesis 2 described, and a preview of what is coming.

The new creation finishes the story. Marriage is a sign pointing beyond itself, and Revelation 19:7-9 shows the whole church as a bride prepared for the wedding supper of the Lamb. There the quiet adornment of the saints is finally seen in full, the fine linen being the righteous acts of the holy ones. The wife who trusted God in a hard house and the husband who honored her will find that the beauty they cultivated in secret was the very thing God had been preparing.

quiz.q: How does Peter say a wife might win an unbelieving husband?

options.text: By her pure and reverent conduct, won over without words.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2: godly behavior can preach where argument cannot.

options.text: By persistently arguing the truth of the gospel.
options.note: Peter points to conduct won without words, not to argument.

options.text: By making herself outwardly attractive.
options.note: He explicitly redirects from outward adornment to inner character.

options.text: By her quiet, godly life that her husband can see.
options.note: True and close, though the answer should name her pure and reverent conduct specifically.

quiz.q: What beauty does Peter say is precious in God's sight?

options.text: The unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit.
options.note: Verse 4: the inner disposition of the heart is what God treasures.

options.text: Carefully arranged hair, jewelry, and fine clothes.
options.note: These are the outward adornment Peter contrasts with true beauty.

options.text: A striking outward appearance that draws attention.
options.note: God prizes the hidden person of the heart, not outward show.

options.text: The inner character of the heart rather than external display.
options.note: True, though the answer should name the gentle and quiet spirit specifically.

quiz.q: Whom does Peter hold up as an example for believing wives?

options.text: Sarah and the holy women of the past who hoped in God.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6: believing wives are Sarah's children when they do what is right.

options.text: The wealthy, admired women of their own society.
options.note: He points away from outward status to the godly women of old.

options.text: The faithful women of Israel's history who trusted God.
options.note: True in spirit, though Peter names Sarah specifically as the model.

options.text: No one in particular; it is only general advice.
options.note: He gives a concrete example, Sarah, and the holy women.

quiz.q: How are husbands to treat their wives?

options.text: With consideration and honor, as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life.
options.note: Verse 7: considerate care and honor rooted in spiritual equality.

options.text: As inferiors who must simply obey.
options.note: The wife is honored as a fellow heir, not treated as an inferior.

options.text: With tenderness, as a precious vessel to be handled carefully.
options.note: True, verse 7, though the answer should include honoring her as a fellow heir.

options.text: However they see fit, since they lead the home.
options.note: Leadership here means considerate honor, not doing as one pleases.

quiz.q: What warning does Peter attach to a husband's treatment of his wife?

options.text: That his prayers may be hindered if he fails to honor her.
options.note: Verse 7: how he treats his wife directly affects his fellowship with God.

options.text: That he may lose his social standing.
options.note: The stake is his relationship with God, not his reputation.

options.text: That his wife may leave him.
options.note: Peter's stated concern is the hindering of his prayers.

options.text: That his communion with God will suffer.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should name the hindering of prayer specifically.

questions: Peter says godly conduct can win others without a word. Whose heart might God be inviting you to reach more by how you live than by what you say?
God treasures a gentle and quiet spirit as unfading beauty. Where do you invest more in outward appearance than in the inner person God prizes?
The holy women hoped in God and did not give way to fear. What fear tends to unsettle you, and what would it look like to anchor your hope in God instead?
Husbands are to honor their wives as fellow heirs of grace. Whether in marriage or other relationships, where are you called to honor someone as a full equal before God?
How we treat those closest to us can even affect our prayers. Is there a relationship in your home that needs mending so that nothing hinders your walk with God?

translationNotes.note: Submit yourselves continues the household teaching from 2:13; the aim here is missionary, that an unbelieving husband may be won by his wife's conduct.
A gentle and quiet spirit renders praus kai hesychios; it denotes settled, meek strength that hopes in God, not timidity or weakness.
Delicate vessel translates the weaker vessel, an image of value and care rather than inferiority; fellow heirs affirms the wife's full equality in the gift of life.
